clue.text: National editor-ial?

blocks.note: C. P. Scott was the long-serving editor of the Manchester Guardian
the suffix -ial means 'relating to', as the suffix -ish does

explanation.surface: A query about some country's national editorial column.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen splits the word: 'editor' is one famous Guardian editor and '-ial' is swapped for an equivalent suffix.
explanation.definitionFit: Scottish describes a nationality, so it serves as an adjective identifying a nation's people.

clue.text: Ed punched by feature writers

indicators.note: a target punched by something has it driven into it, so one piece lodges inside the other

blocks.note: Ed Balls, the Labour politician
a point is a feature or detail, as in 'a good point'

explanation.surface: A man called Ed is assaulted by journalists who write features.
explanation.walkthrough: Ed Balls was a UK Labour cabinet minister; POINT goes inside his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballpoints are pens, things that write, so the plural noun matches an everyday term for implements of writing.

clue.text: Bit of a bloomer over deliveries found outside residence

indicators.note: lying outside another word means wrapping around it

blocks.note: a cricket over consists of six balls bowled
a pad is slang for someone's home

explanation.surface: Part of a bloomer turns up around a house after cricket balls are bowled.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is a fixed set of balls bowled, so 'over deliveries' is a number; 'bloomer' suggests knickers or a loaf but means a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: A spadix is the fleshy flower spike of plants such as arum lilies, a part of a flowering plant.

clue.text: Political journalist about right for Ed

indicators.note: about means around, so the journalist's name goes round the other piece

blocks.note: Robert Peston, the British political broadcaster
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A political journalist covers matters on the right on behalf of someone named Ed.
explanation.walkthrough: PESTON goes around R, the one-letter addition turning one journalist into another.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Preston was a long-serving editor of the Guardian, and Ed is a short form of editor.

clue.text: A single friend a joker set up, hot little thing

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means raised, so the string is read from the bottom upward

blocks.note: a single one
a pal is a friend
taken as written
J is the abbreviation for a joker on playing cards

explanation.surface: Someone sets up a lonely friend on a date with a comedian, an attractive little thing.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'set up' reads the whole string from the bottom upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A jalapeño is a small spicy chilli pepper, so it's a little thing that is hot in the mouth.

clue.text: Last seen of beautiful colour arising in film I relish

indicators.note: what is seen last of a word is its final letter
in a down clue, rising up means the letters read from bottom to top
the risen piece is placed inside the following words

blocks.note: pic is short for picture, a film
final letter of the word
lilac is a pale purple colour
taken as written

explanation.surface: A beautiful colour rising up on screen gives a moviegoer pleasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relish' looks like a verb meaning enjoy, but it's the condiment.
explanation.definitionFit: Piccalilli is a yellow mustard pickle of chopped vegetables, a kind of relish served as a condiment.

clue.text: Article penned by Ed, more self-obsessed

indicators.note: penned means enclosed as in a pen, so the article sits inside the editor's name

blocks.note: Katharine Viner, editor of the Guardian
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An editor writes a piece about someone growing more narcissistic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' sounds like a newspaper piece, but it's the grammatical article.
explanation.definitionFit: Vain describes excessive pride in oneself, so the comparative form expresses greater narcissism.

clue.text: Son John, dogged competitor

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
john and crapper are both slang for a toilet

explanation.surface: A man introduces his son John as a determined rival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'John' looks like the son's name but is American slang for a lavatory.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrapper is someone who fights hard and refuses to give up, a tenacious fighter.

clue.text: Soul discovered in pressman, I’m astounded!

indicators.note: something discovered within the following words is found lying inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the word boundaries

explanation.surface: A reporter exclaims in amazement at finding a soul.
explanation.definitionFit: Anima is the Latin and Jungian term for the inner self or spirit of a person.

clue.text: Greek letter followed by second in alphabet, and the others

indicators.note: the second letter of the following word is the one taken

blocks.note: eta is the seventh letter of the Greek alphabet
its second letter

explanation.surface: A lesson on the Greek alphabet, one letter after another, and all the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second in alphabet' looks like B, but it means the second letter of the word itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Et al. is the Latin abbreviation for et alii, used in citations to cover remaining authors.

clue.text: Detachment taking steps to cordon off one street

indicators.note: a cordon surrounds an area, so the first piece encloses the next ones

blocks.note: dancing is moving the feet in steps
Roman numeral one
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A police detachment acts to seal off a single street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detachment' suggests a unit of police or troops, but it's the abstract noun for keeping aloof.
explanation.definitionFit: Distancing is keeping oneself apart emotionally, the same aloofness that detachment names.

clue.text: Onto exercise that’s a mistake, pour – this?

definitions.text: Onto exercise that’s a mistake, pour – this?

blocks.note: to tip a liquid is to pour it
physical education, school exercise
a cross marks an answer as wrong

explanation.surface: A teacher's instruction: spill this onto any wrong answer in the exercise book.
explanation.walkthrough: TIP is put onto PE and X; the whole clue also describes what you do with the product. Tipp-Ex is a British brand of correction fluid.
explanation.definitionFit: Tipp-Ex is white correction fluid painted over written errors, so the whole clue describes its use.

clue.text: Forward company in snuggle bug

indicators.note: in places the company abbreviation within the endearment

blocks.note: both are terms of endearment for a darling
CO is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A cuddly little darling is pushing forward into company.
explanation.definitionFit: Forward can describe a child advanced for their age, the sense of developing early ahead of peers.

clue.text: More than noble operation

blocks.note: over means more than, as in over ten
a lord is a nobleman

explanation.surface: A procedure described as nobler than noble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Operation' suggests surgery, but it is a military campaign.
explanation.definitionFit: Operation Overlord was the Allied codename for the 1944 Normandy invasion, a famous military campaign.

clue.text: Ultimately wanting paper published, Ed

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, and ultimately points at the end of the word

blocks.note: a sheet of paper
a newspaper ran a story when it published it

explanation.surface: An editor called Ed, ultimately short of a newspaper to print.
explanation.walkthrough: Among the editors, this Ed is Ed Sheeran, the singer-songwriter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ed Sheeran is the English pop singer, so his first name stands for him in a clue.

clue.text: Everything’s great when everyone dandy

blocks.note: all means everyone
a swell is a fashionably dressed man, like a dandy

explanation.surface: Life is good when everybody's doing fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dandy' reads as an adjective meaning fine, but it's the noun for a dapper man.
explanation.definitionFit: All's well is a stock phrase saying that matters are going satisfactorily, with no problems at all.

clue.text: Ed, prune

blocks.note: first meaning: Stephen ..., editor of the Jewish Chronicle
second meaning: to cut a tree back hard to its trunk

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ed' here is an abbreviation for editor, one of the many newspaper editors in this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Pollarding trees means lopping branches back to the trunk, while Stephen Pollard edited a London weekly newspaper.

clue.text: Trains on time I report on the radio?

indicators.note: on the radio something is heard rather than seen, so the word is spelled by its sound

blocks.note: re means on or concerning
T is the abbreviation for time
taken as written
a report is a piece of news

explanation.surface: A broadcaster reads out a railway update that trains are on time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trains' looks like railway services, but it means trailing entourages.
explanation.definitionFit: A train can be a line of attendants following an important person, which is also what a retinue is.

clue.text: Sign one’s invested in resurrection of old Italian newspaper

indicators.note: to invest something in is to put it inside, so one goes within
a resurrection is a rising up, which in a down clue reads the letters upward

blocks.note: Latin was the language of ancient Italy
the i is a British national newspaper
I is the Roman numeral one; the 's is read as 'is'

explanation.surface: A newspaper story about reviving an old Italian paper and investing in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The i is a British daily newspaper. LATIN plus I goes upward, then the second I is slipped in.
explanation.definitionFit: To initial a document is to sign it with the first letters of one's names.

clue.text: The Beckham Rusbridger uncovered?

blocks.note: first meaning: the eldest son of David and Victoria Beckham
second meaning: strip the outer letters from the name of Alan Rusbridger, a former Guardian editor, and you read US BRIDGE

explanation.walkthrough: Removing the cover letters of Rusbridger leaves 'usbridge', read as a US bridge, an example of which is in New York.
explanation.definitionFit: Brooklyn Beckham is the footballer's son, and the Brooklyn Bridge is the famous New York crossing over the East River.

clue.text: Corruption of editor was revolting?

indicators.note: corrupting something distorts its form, so the letters of the next word are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An editor's corruption was disgusting, or caused a revolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' tempts as disgusting; here it means rising in revolt.
explanation.definitionFit: To riot is to engage in violent public disorder, which is what people in revolt do.

clue.text: See 2 Down
One partial to drivel – Morgan, say?

indicators.note: being partial to means taking a part in, so the first piece sits within the other

blocks.note: prate is foolish chatter
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Piers Morgan, the tabloid editor and broadcaster, is fond of talking nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: Morgan suggests Piers Morgan among the editors, but this is Henry Morgan, the Welsh buccaneer.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Henry Morgan was a 17th-century privateer raiding Spanish colonies in the Caribbean, an example of a seafaring robber.

clue.text: Certain two jerks making a splash?

indicators.note: jerking something shakes it about, so the preceding letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A pair of fools are certain to make a big impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making a splash' suggests attracting attention; the definition is a small dash of mixer.
explanation.definitionFit: A splash is a small quantity of liquid added to a drink, like a mixer added to gin.

clue.text: Number coming into Hastings from an island

indicators.note: coming into means entering, so the number goes inside the editor's first name

blocks.note: Max Hastings, former editor of the Daily Telegraph
N is the abbreviation for number

explanation.surface: A number of people arrive in the seaside town of Hastings from an island.
explanation.walkthrough: Hastings is a south-coast English town, but here it's the surname of the editor, so his first name is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Manx is the adjective for the Isle of Man, describing people or things belonging there.

clue.text: Network essential to James Harding

indicators.note: what is essential lies at the heart, so the letters sit inside the name that follows

blocks.note: the letters span the two names

explanation.surface: A broadcasting network relies on its editor James Harding.
explanation.walkthrough: James Harding edited The Times and later ran BBC News.
explanation.definitionFit: A mesh is an interlaced net of threads or wires, a structure of connected strands.

clue.text: Endless worry accompanying European correspondent

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is removed from the following word

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
a qualm is a pang of worry or doubt

explanation.surface: A foreign correspondent in Europe has endless anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Correspondent' suggests a reporter, but it means a counterpart that corresponds.
explanation.definitionFit: A correspondent can be something that corresponds to another, a match or peer of the same standing.

clue.text: Confirmed date arranged when screening match

indicators.note: arranging puts things in an order, so the preceding letters are re-sorted
screening something hides it behind, so the first piece wraps the next

blocks.note: taken as written
a Test is an international cricket match

explanation.surface: A date is fixed while a match is being shown on television.
explanation.walkthrough: A Test match is an international cricket game lasting up to five days.
explanation.definitionFit: To attest is to bear witness that something is true, so attested means formally verified.
